tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

## 598adf58-4d0d-4866-82b2-42a10512e240

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.  "description": "In 2018, the Wake Forest Pitching Lab was just the dream of an Orthopedic surgeon and a head baseball coach. By January 2019, that dream was becoming a reality. We opened a biomechanics lab dedicated to baseball pitching, full of technology and tools, but also an impressive team of experts. Over the last seven years, the lab has gained a reputation for leading baseball pitching biomechanics research and utilizing data for injury prevention and player development. In this Competitive Advantage talk, we will discuss the history of the lab, how we have leveraged data for success, and explore what's next.",
 "chapters": null,

 "title": "SSAC26: When the Model Meets Human: The Future of Basketball Decision Making",
 "channel": "42 Analytics",
 "upload_date": "20260409",
 "duration": 2681,
 "view_count": 1009,
 "description": "Basketball analytics has evolved far beyond shot charts and efficiency metrics. Today's teams operate in an era of player-tracking data, biomechanical modeling, and emerging AI systems capable of influencing decisions in real time. But as data becomes more powerful, new questions emerge: What aspects of basketball can truly be modeled, and what still relies on human instinct? Are teams optimizing for winning or merely for avoiding mistakes? And how do players experience a game increasingly shaped by algorithms behind the scenes? This panel brings together leaders from coaching, front offices, player personnel, and the court itself to explore how analytics is actually used inside modern basketball organizations. As AI enters the next phase of sports decision-making, this conversation asks a bigger question: Is the future of basketball driven by better models, or by better understanding of the people who play the game?",

In surgery, treatment guidelines are created through evidence-based methods, while in sports, gameplans are derived from film-review, statistics and scouting reports. Despite the wealth of data available to surgeons and sports teams, surgical guidelines and sports gameplans are not always followed. Decision-making often relies on something that is not captured in the numbers, and emotions often compete with evidence. Surgery can serve as a lens for sports teams to understand how data influences high-stakes decisions and ways to effectively integrate emotion with evidence.",

# Applications: The Future of Peak Performance (Wu Tsai and Donahoe)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Hamstring re-injury is the closest match to Baylor football. The talk describes a roughly 10-minute video-based exercise series at Stanford football practice that feeds a digital-twin estimate of hamstring injury or re-injury likelihood and rehab stage [15:26]. Baylor could treat this as a candidate second opinion beside its existing return-to-play hamstring work (targeted groups, joint-specific isometric testing), not as a replacement.
- Inference: The ACL example (high-speed video, about 10 minutes per athlete, a named weak link such as hip or knee, then individualized training) [13:54, 14:24] maps to Baylor women's sports (basketball, volleyball, soccer, lacrosse-type programs are the ones Donahoe lists). The decision it informs is which athlete gets extra hip or knee strengthening emphasis in a team block.
- Inference: The gender data gap (only 6% of sports science studies exclusively on women [17:30]) is a reason to be cautious when applying force plate or GPS norms built mostly on male samples to Baylor women's teams. The decision is whether a team uses its own athletes' history as the reference instead of a published norm.
- Inference: The data-sharing model the panel describes (leagues supply multi-season player data, academics build models, private companies build dashboards) [43:28] is a template for asking what Baylor data, stripped of identifiers, could be offered to a university research partner.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Injury risk "can be reduced, not eliminated" through progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine, with no promise of injury prevention. The talk extends and partly conflicts: Donahoe says the aim is to reduce likelihood [14:56], which agrees, but Wu Tsai frames the goal as telling an athlete what will happen to the body before it does [32:17, 42:58], which goes further than the baseline allows.
- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric in the corpus. The talk describes one (digital twin), so it extends rather than conflicts.
- Eric's baseline: NordBord was retired roster-wide but kept for small return-to-play groups with clear clinical purpose and dedicated oversight. The talk's 10-minute hamstring screen [15:26] is a different method with the same logic of a targeted group, so it is comparable, not contradictory.
- Eric's baseline: Data collection is judged on cost versus insight. The talk's "two iPhones" setup [12:21] claims low collection cost, which the baseline would accept only if the output changes a decision.

## What would have to be true

- Published validation: the speakers say it is too early to see fewer ACL injuries after about a year [14:56]. Before Baylor acts, there should be peer-reviewed accuracy data (sensitivity, false-positive rate) for the hamstring and ACL twins, which this talk does not give.
- A sample of athletes similar to Baylor's (college football, college women's sports) in the model's training data.
- Athletic Medicine agreement on who owns the output and what a "high propensity" result triggers.
- Video capture that Baylor staff can repeat exactly (same exercises, camera setup), consistent with the baseline on repeatable protocols.

## Do not apply when

- The vendor or institute has not shown prediction accuracy in an external sample. The talk is from the funder and the athletic director of the partner institution, so both have a stake in the result.
- The output would be used as a selection or playing-time filter for an athlete with no clinical follow-up.
- The claim is being borrowed for a general population: Wu Tsai's benefit claims for youth and everyday athletes [41:28] were not tested in the talk.
- The athlete data would leave Baylor without a data-sharing agreement and consent process.

## First step

Ask Athletic Medicine whether they know of published accuracy data for the digital-twin hamstring and ACL screens the talk describes. Do not collect any new data until that is answered.

- Inference: The ACL example (high-speed video, about 10 minutes per athlete, a named weak link such as hip or knee, then individualized training) [13:54, 14:24] maps to Baylor women's sports (basketball, volleyball, soccer, lacrosse-type programs are the ones Donahoe lists). The decision it informs is which athlete gets extra hip or knee strengthening emphasis in a team block.
- Inference: The gender data gap (only 6% of sports science studies exclusively on women [17:30]) is a reason to be cautious when applying force plate or GPS norms built mostly on male samples to Baylor women's teams. The decision is whether a team uses its own athletes' history as the reference instead of a published norm.
- Inference: The data-sharing model the panel describes (leagues supply multi-season player data, academics build models, private companies build dashboards) [43:28] is a template for asking what Baylor data, stripped of identifiers, could be offered to a university research partner.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Injury risk "can be reduced, not eliminated" through progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine, with no promise of injury prevention. The talk's surprise (pelvis rotation velocity fell in the best pitches) is a reminder to check direction, not assume more is better.
- Inference: N-of-1 modeling, with an individual expected-performance line adjusted for rest and travel [18:40, 19:41], is relevant to Baylor travel weeks: an athlete's own daily jump metric against his own trend, adjusted for travel days, instead of a team average.
- Inference: The standing meeting of biomechanics, coaches, athletic trainers, strength coaches and analytics [12:27, 22:18] matches a recurring Applied Performance, Athletic Medicine and coaching review of the same data, with one agreed plan per athlete.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Force plate metric selection follows output, driver, strategy and optional symmetry metrics, with "fluffy" metrics added only with a rationale (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics). The talk's structure agrees and extends it to an outdoor sport with motion capture.
- Eric's baseline: Mission is to enable the high-performance team to answer and ask better questions. The talk's team meetings agree.
- Eric's baseline: Mod RSI from daily CMJ was chosen as a daily readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable. The talk's individual-baseline approach extends this, since it uses each athlete's own trend.
- Eric's baseline: A demanding test is kept only where there is a small group, a clear clinical purpose and dedicated oversight; collection has to be sustainable. The lab's marker-based system was replaced by markerless capture in 2022 to allow regular use [12:27], which agrees with this reasoning.
- Eric's baseline: Protocols must be exactly repeatable. The talk does not say how markerless capture repeatability was checked.

## What would have to be true

- For football, a normative database first. Nicholson says her own lab needed 2020 to 2022 to build norms and that quarterback data does not have an equivalent [23:19].
- Enough repeated trials per athlete to draw a stable individual trend line (the talk does not give a minimum).
- Clear agreement on who acts on a flag: strength staff, athletic trainers or Athletic Medicine.
- Capture hardware that works in Baylor's real practice setting, which the talk solves with markerless cameras in a bullpen and stadium.

## Do not apply when

- The claim is causal: the pelvis rotation result came from one fall season with no intervention [24:20], and the speaker says she has not explored why.
- The results are used to justify a program: the injury-free seasons and draft numbers [15:33, 16:04] are one program's counts with no comparison group, and the speaker has a stake.
- Applying baseball pitching findings to football throwing or kicking without sport-specific norms; she says she lacks the expertise to say what to fix for quarterbacks [23:19].
- Samples are small: n-of-1 models and single-fall comparisons need enough repeated efforts per athlete.

## First step

Pick one recurring football task with repeated trials (for example a sprint or jump test across a training block) and, for one position group, list which of the existing Baylor metrics would be output, driver and strategy metrics. No new collection needed.

# Applications: When the Model Meets Human (Basketball Decision Making panel)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Raman's first filter for a new metric (is it actionable for a player, what is the context, does it relate to winning, does it fit our roster) [03:36, 04:07, 04:37] is a checklist Baylor could run on any new PFF grade, GPS metric or force plate metric before it is added to a report.
- Inference: McNair's practice of sorting decisions by how much the data can be trusted (unimpeachable versus suggestive) [11:12] fits recruiting grading: the PFF grade leads where it is stable, and scouting or film leads where it is weak, with the split written down per position.
- Inference: Sending scouts to watch film to explain an odd number (for example a low assist rate) [12:43] applies to an odd GPS or force plate number: a coach reviews film to explain it before the number is acted on.
- Inference: The panel's advice on trust, starting with near-certain calls and moving to closer ones over a season [28:31, 29:02], and on involving players in the plan [32:05], applies to how Applied Performance introduces a new metric to position coaches and athletes.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: a trained "coach's eye" matters "at least as much" as technology for daily assessment, yet Eric's own writing replaced subjective wellness surveys with an objective mod RSI from force plates. The corpus flags this as an unresolved tension. The panel's position (data supplies information, a person still chooses [25:25]) sits on the coach's-eye side and does not settle it.
- Eric's baseline: Reject ownership language ("my team, my athletes"). The panel's "we all own the result together" [30:03] agrees.
- Eric's baseline: Data collection is judged on cost versus insight. The panel does not discuss collection cost, so there is no direct link there.
- Eric's baseline: The department enables Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine to answer their own questions rather than handing down answers. The panel's emphasis on embedded staff (McNair full-time in Houston, Raman on the coaching staff) [31:04] agrees.

## What would have to be true

- A named person at Baylor who is in the room with coaches regularly, not only at report time, before trust is assumed.
- For any metric, a check against Baylor data: retroactive comparison to results, as Raman describes [04:07].
- Agreement with coaches ahead of the game or week on when a model input applies, as Raman describes doing before the game rather than reading a report mid-game [23:53].

## Do not apply when

- The panel's examples are NBA and WNBA decisions with pro-level tracking data; Baylor football lacks that tracking data and roster turnover is different.
- The story of a single playoff series outcome is used as evidence for or against a model; McNair's own point is that a small sample should not change the plan [28:31].
- An athlete-facing number would be presented as a verdict on confidence or likability; the panel says confidence is not reliably measured [15:13] and the coachability scale is "rough" [21:20].
- Applying a player's (Adams) opinion that some metrics are overblown [08:10] to decide whether to drop a metric. It is one player's view.

## First step

Take the next new metric someone proposes and run it past Raman's four questions in writing (actionable, context, relation to winning, fit to our roster) before it goes into any staff report.

# Applications: Surgery and Sports (Naples)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Time-of-day effects [13:19] suggest logging the clock time of every VALD jump test and GPS session and checking, after a semester, whether metrics drift by time slot. The decision it informs is whether testing should be fixed to one time slot.
- Inference: Team familiarity [10:15, 10:45] can be read as a tester or coach-staffing question: when a different staff member runs force plate or sprint testing, is data noisier than with the usual staff? Baylor could record who administered each test.
- Inference: Travel and circadian effects [11:47, 12:18] apply to away-game weeks: compare post-travel jump or readiness values with home-week values for the same athletes.
- Inference: Exploring outliers rather than discarding them [16:25] applies to GPS spike cleaning: log what was removed and why, then review the removed records for a pattern.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Testing has to be exactly repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). The talk extends this: time of day and tester familiarity are additional things that should be held constant or recorded.
- Eric's baseline: Do not reassess an athlete with known fatigue (from the assessment manual, author uncertain). The talk's travel and circadian points fit the same thinking but give no athlete data.
- Eric's baseline: The Playbook documents GPS data cleaning with spike detection. The talk's advice to explore outliers conflicts in emphasis: cleaning removes them, the talk says to study them. They can be reconciled by keeping a log of removed spikes.
- Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data." The talk is consistent with that, since it argues hidden context changes outcomes.

## What would have to be true

- Enough repeated tests per athlete, at recorded times, to see a time-of-day pattern; the talk gives no sample size for a sports setting.
- The time, tester and travel fields actually captured in the athlete management system, not only in notes.
- Comparisons between athletes avoided; use within-athlete comparisons.

## Do not apply when

- The evidence is surgical and the claim is being carried across without testing it in athletes: the birthday, cardiac team-familiarity and cancer timing studies were medical and only described, not named.
- A p-value-free reading is used as permission to act on noise: Naples says "not significant" is not the same as "not relevant" [15:53], but he gives no rule for deciding.
- Naples himself notes his Halloween example has no data [05:39].
- Time of day is confounded with practice schedule or sport demands that the athletes cannot change.

## First step

For the next two weeks of testing, add two fields to the existing test log: clock time and tester name. Review after the block; no change to how tests are run.

=== FILE: videos/2026-04-09_sehodnyt3ko_the-future-of-peak-performance-clara-wu-tsai-and-john-donaho/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: sehodnyt3ko
title: "SSAC26: The Future of Peak Performance: Clara Wu Tsai and John Donahoe"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Clara Wu Tsai, John Donahoe, Jessica Gelman (moderator), Sarah Buck (introduction)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, policy]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated conversation between Clara Wu Tsai (owner of the New York Liberty, founder of the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance) and John Donahoe (Stanford athletic director, former Nike CEO). They describe a research alliance that studies people at peak health and aims to predict injury, personalize training, and close the data gap on female athletes. Stanford is presented as the lab for applying it. Donahoe also lays out a three-part rule set he wants for college athletics. The injury-prediction work is described by its own funder and partner, and Donahoe says it is too early to show fewer injuries.

## Key claims

- Moving the Liberty to Barclays Center in Brooklyn was the most transformative change, followed by investing in facilities, performance and player experience on the same terms as the men's team [02:06].
- Wu Tsai says owning the teams showed how much is unknown about the human body, and that most health research studies disease rather than peak performance [10:51, 11:21].
- The alliance was created to study people at peak health and ask how top performers move, adapt, fatigue and recover [11:51].
- Wu Tsai says digital twins grounded in biomechanics and physiology can predict injury, personalize training and simulate performance, using simple video from two iPhones [12:21].
- Stanford and the alliance chose ACL injuries and hamstring injuries as the two areas to push through first [13:24].
- Donahoe describes the ACL process: high-speed video of an athlete (about 10 minutes) produces a digital twin that estimates her ACL injury propensity and points to a specific weak link, shared with the athlete and trainer for targeted training [13:54, 14:24, 14:56].
- Donahoe says it is too early to show a measurable drop in injuries after about a year, but athletes, coaches and trainers like it [14:56].
- For hamstrings, researchers film football players doing a series of exercises, and the twin estimates injury or re-injury likelihood and rehab stage [15:26].
- Wu Tsai says closing the gender gap in physiology and performance knowledge is a priority, and launched a women's health institute (WHISPER) in Boston in January, run by Dr. Kate Ackerman [17:30, 18:00, 18:30].
- Donahoe says a Stanford event co-sponsored with Wu Tsai drew 400 people, and that Stanford can act as a lab with 900 student athletes [19:01, 20:32].
- Donahoe says over 200 faculty work with Wu Tsai on sports science, and gives mental wellness as an example of faculty collaborating who otherwise would not [21:33, 22:03].
- Donahoe says college athletics is in a "lawless middle" and proposes eligibility rules, transfer portal limits, and a salary cap with transparency [23:34, 24:36, 25:07].
- Donahoe says Stanford will double down on Olympic and women's sports and launch an endowment campaign [26:39, 27:09].
- Wu Tsai names three unsolved challenges: predicting injuries before they happen, individualizing training and recovery, and the data gap in women's physiology [31:46, 32:17, 32:47].
- Donahoe says all the alliance research is open and shared across institutions [38:24].
- Wu Tsai says the biggest breakthrough would come from combining league player data, academic models and private-sector mobile dashboards to tell athletes what will happen and what to do [42:58, 43:28].

## Numbers and definitions

- Only 6% of sports science studies are done exclusively on women (Wu Tsai) [17:30].
- ACL injuries are "four to six times more likely" in women; Donahoe says he looked this up on ChatGPT and that it varies by sport [13:54].
- Alliance described by the moderator: seven core institutions, hundreds of collaborations, more than 500 publications, multiple therapeutics advancing toward FDA approval [10:21].
- ACL and hamstring screens: about 10 minutes of video each [13:54, 15:26].
- Over 200 Stanford faculty involved [21:33]; 900 student athletes, 36 sports [25:38]; 400 attended the event [19:01].
- About 59 Stanford students and alumni at the Paris Olympics; Directors' Cup won 25 years straight [07:13].
- Donahoe estimates college basketball as one third professionalized and two thirds college [26:08].
- Alliance about five years old, launched 2020; teams acquired 2019 [10:21, 10:51].
- Athletes now play at most into the mid-40s, depending on sport (Wu Tsai) [44:31].
- Captions are garbled in places (for example "Wyss Institute", "Woo Sai", "Oura" for what is likely a leadership body); no number appears garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Digital twin: AI-based model of an athlete's biomechanics and physiology built from video, used for injury propensity and rehab stage [14:24, 15:26].
- Precision exercise medicine, based on molecular biology of exercise (Salk Institute) [28:10, 28:42].
- Regenerative rehabilitation (University of Oregon) [29:14].
- Open, multi-institution research network convened by the alliance [38:24].

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy, sensitivity or false-positive data are shown for the ACL or hamstring twins; Donahoe says results on injury rates are too early [14:56].
- The two main speakers are the funder and the partner institution's athletic director, so benefit claims are institutional views.
- The "four to six times" figure was looked up by the speaker on a chatbot and not sourced.
- Claims that the work helps youth and everyday athletes [35:22, 41:28] were not tested in the talk.
- Claim of a "digital twin" that tells an athlete what will happen before it does is a stated goal, not a shown result [32:17].

## Q&A

- No audience questions were captured; the moderator asked quick-hit questions at the end.
- Liberty international games in 10 years: at least one a year [40:27].
- Where AI will drive most insight: fans, athletes and leaders; Wu Tsai expects immersive fan experiences and injury-avoidance benefits for young athletes [40:57, 41:28].
- Who uses alliance research in 2036: both gold medalists and youth parents [41:58].
- Biggest possible breakthrough: injury prediction with guidance, built from league data, academic models and private dashboards [42:58].
- Will athletes play longer: both hope so [44:31].

## Summary

Dr. Kristen Nicholson, director of the Wake Forest pitching lab, tells how the lab was built to reduce elbow (UCL) injuries without losing pitch velocity. Motion-capture data from Wake Forest pitchers and community visitors produced a short list of injury and performance indicators, many of which overlap. She shows a player case, best-versus-worst fastball comparisons, and program results (no major arm injuries in three seasons, more drafted pitchers). She describes the next step, individual (n of 1) models that track fatigue, travel and rest. The results are one program's outcomes without a comparison group.

## Key claims

- UCL injuries have risen sharply, including in younger players; she cites a ninefold increase in non-surgical UCL injuries from 2009 to 2018 [00:36].
- The lab started in 2018 from an orthopedic surgeon's idea, with the head baseball coach, and opened to the community as well as the team [02:06, 03:37].
- The lab's value is the collaboration among biomechanists, sports medicine, coaches, athletic trainers and strength coaches [03:07, 03:37].
- Pitchers need high velocity with low shoulder and elbow load, but optimal mechanics are hard to define because pitchers differ [05:09].
- From large data sets the lab identified key injury indicators and key performance indicators, and many were the same, which she links to pitching efficiency [06:11, 06:42].
- Maximum humeral rotation velocity and elbow extension velocity were the largest influences on pitch velocity; ground reaction force and trunk timing also related [06:42].
- In a case example, corrective work on core strength and rotation raised ground reaction force and lined it up through the center of mass [09:20, 09:52].
- The lab published over 20 manuscripts from 2019 to 2022, and she says baseball biomechanics papers nearly doubled in 2020 to 2021 and a baseball biomechanics society formed [10:56].
- Every MLB team has visited or held a video call; nine were strongly influenced [11:26, 11:57].
- Markerless motion capture from 2022 allows regular use in the bullpen and stadium, and data on nearly every high-intent pitch [11:57, 12:27, 12:57].
- In a fall comparison of top versus bottom quartile fastballs, all key variables differed except maximum pelvis rotation velocity, which fell as performance rose; she attributes this to better lead leg blocking and energy transfer [13:28, 13:59].
- Pairing TrackMan ball data with motion capture on a single bullpen showed what differed between good and bad pitches [14:31, 15:02].
- Wake Forest had no major arm injuries in 2022, 2024 and 2025 and reached the postseason each year from 2022 [15:33].
- The lab helped recruit top pitchers, and she says the pitching also helps recruit hitters [16:34, 17:06].
- Next steps: add fatigue and physiological variables, study biomechanics and command, and use n of 1 models [17:36, 18:08, 18:40].
- In an n of 1 model, expected performance is adjusted for travel, rest and workload, and she shows how coaches could adjust rest after an underperforming game [18:40, 19:41, 20:13].

## Numbers and definitions

- Ninefold increase in non-surgical UCL injuries, 2009 to 2018 [00:36].
- 2.5% of Division 1 baseball players had UCL reconstruction in 2017 [00:36].
- Almost 14,000 UCL injuries and 1,400 surgeries, 2013 to 2015 [01:06].
- Median age of surgery patients fell from 20 to 18 [01:06]; nearly one in four high school players will have a UCL injury by graduation [01:06].
- Lab equipment: 12 optical motion capture cameras, three force plates, four high-speed video cameras, TrackMan Pro [02:37].
- Ribbon cutting January 2019 [03:37].
- Seven key injury indicators and 10 key performance indicators [06:11].
- Successful pitchers produce two to two and a half times body weight in ground reaction force [09:20].
- Case player: ground reaction force from 1.9 to 2.2 times body weight [09:52].
- Over 20 manuscripts, 2019 to 2022 [10:56].
- Wake Forest pitchers drafted: 1.7 per year (2010 to 2018) versus 3.4 per year (2019 to 2024) [16:04].
- First round pitcher picks in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 [16:04].
- Early-season pitcher left in through about 65 pitches; late-season pitcher left at about 35, which the speaker says she cannot read on the slide, so the 35 is unreliable [19:10].
- A later example pitcher threw almost 100 pitches above expected [20:13].
- "N of 1 modeling": an individual rather than a group model [18:08].
- The "14,000" and the 2013 to 2015 dates come from auto captions and could be garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Marker-based motion capture, then markerless (computer vision) capture in 2022 [04:07, 12:27].
- Ground reaction force and kinematic sequencing analysis [09:20, 10:23].
- TrackMan ball flight data paired with biomechanics [14:31].
- N of 1 modeling with expected versus observed performance lines adjusted for game travel and rest [18:40, 19:41].
- Regular team meetings across disciplines, mostly in the fall, plus weekly data reviews in season [22:18].

## Limits and open questions

- Program results (injury-free seasons, postseason, draft counts) are one school's counts with no comparison group, told by the lab's director.
- Pelvis rotation finding is one fall, no intervention; she says she has not explored the cause [24:20].
- She states the n of 1 examples are "based on real data" but illustrative of how it might be used, not a finished result [20:13].
- The talk studies biomechanics, not fatigue or travel, so far [17:36].
- No football norms exist in her lab; she collected quarterback and kicker data but lacks the expertise to say what to change [23:19].

## Q&A

- Hitters: markerless capture can also track hitters on the field, including torso rotation and swing plane [21:15].
- Coordination: the whole team meets at least twice a year, mostly fall; she meets the pitching coach and player development coordinator regularly in season [22:18].
- Football quarterbacks: the lab collected quarterback and kicker data, but the database and expertise are missing [23:19].
- Pelvic rotation and balance work: the data was from last fall with no intervention; pre and post data could be reviewed [24:20].
- ACL prevention: outside her expertise; she notes much published work exists on lower extremity motion capture [25:22].

## Summary

A panel of a front-office advisor, a 76ers personnel executive, a WNBA head coach and an NBA player, moderated by Shane Battier, on how models and human judgment meet in basketball. The panelists say tracking data now explains things players and coaches already knew, that a new metric has to be actionable and fit the roster, and that models give information rather than answers. Much of the discussion is about trust: embedded analysts, small-sample outcomes, and getting players to buy in. The player on the panel says players mostly treat data as a guideline. The views are the panelists' own experience, with few numbers.

## Key claims

- Battier says data is now like oxygen, and that analytics has moved from what happened toward how it happens [01:34, 02:04].
- McNair says skeletal tracking lets teams measure what players and coaches already knew, such as contested rebounds and carving out space; the early data had only a dot for each player location [02:36, 03:06].
- Raman tests a new metric for whether it is actionable for a player, the context behind it, whether it correlates with winning, and whether it fits her own roster [03:36, 04:07, 04:37].
- Battier says the most used phrase in NBA data rooms is that all models are wrong and some are useful [05:08].
- Antonian says G League data and analyst support are behind the NBA, and basketball is behind baseball on biomechanics for player development [05:38, 06:08].
- Antonian says the G League is used to test ideas (lineups, shot volume) before taking them to the NBA staff [06:39, 07:10].
- Adams says the screening "gravity" credit is a little overblown in his view, and that screening comes down to communication with the ball handler [08:10, 08:41, 09:11].
- McNair says he goes with data where it is nearly unimpeachable and leans on the eye test where it is only suggestive, and that scouts can be pointed to what the data cannot yet measure [11:12, 11:42, 12:13].
- When a number looks odd, such as a low assist rate, the staff watches film to test theories [12:43, 13:13].
- Raman says the coaching staff sets OKRs with analysts and the front office, and that she has not seen confidence measured reliably; over-indexing on numbers can make a player second-guess [14:13, 15:13, 15:44].
- Antonian says athleticism (how someone moves) is the thing she most needs to see live [16:46, 17:16, 17:46].
- Adams advises young bigs to lean toward defensive and off-ball work because scoring roles are volatile, and to listen for whether teammates like playing with them [18:48, 19:18, 19:48].
- Antonian says teams gather coachability information and try to rate it, though roughly [21:20, 21:50].
- Raman says lineup choices depend on the game situation and are planned before the game, not driven by a mid-game AI report [22:52, 23:22, 23:53].
- Antonian says data often gives a list of issues rather than one answer, and coaches must choose which to fix in game [24:54, 25:25].
- Adams says players tend to treat analytics as a guideline and many do not want it while playing [26:29, 27:00].
- McNair describes a playoff series where a player hit his first three threes after the plan was to help off him; the coaches kept the plan, and he says that trust in coaches matters more than a small-sample result [28:01, 28:31].
- Panelists say to start with near-certain (90-10) recommendations and move to closer calls as trust builds [28:31, 29:02].
- Antonian and Raman say relationships and staff who are embedded full time build the trust needed [29:32, 31:04, 31:34].
- Panelists describe involving players early, including asking defenders about coverage, for buy-in [32:05, 32:35, 33:06].
- McNair tells of a Houston player who explained that crashing the glass every time costs energy for defense, which refined the model [34:37, 35:07].
- McNair says better models mostly find things players already do that win games, and find them with more certainty and the right magnitude [36:39].
- McNair says front offices should get familiar with large language models, including what they are bad at, and use them now [42:20, 42:51, 43:23].
- A panelist says the tension between transition defense and offensive rebounding could not be resolved until tracking data arrived [43:55].

## Numbers and definitions

- Early tracking data was a dot for the first "7 8 years" (McNair) [03:06].
- Hypothetical: a player passes "60% more" if pushed left, given by Adams as an illustration [26:29].
- Playoff example: three threes in the first three attempts of the series [28:01]; 90-10, 80-20, 70-30 and 51-49 calls used as a scale of difficulty [28:31, 29:02].
- PJ Tucker example: playing 38 minutes at a high level [34:37].
- Antonian says teams have "eight different problems" on average [25:25].
- McNair has spent eight months on AI in his sabbatical year [42:51].
- Garbled: a G League three-point volume ("53s per game... some amount of threes") is unclear in the captions [07:10].
- "Screening gravity" and "force of impact" are named as metrics but not defined [07:40, 08:10].

## Methods and frameworks named

- 3D skeletal player tracking [02:04, 03:06].
- Retroactive testing of a new metric against league results [04:07].
- OKRs co-set by coaches, analysts and front office [14:13].
- Coachability rating scale built from information across a player's previous stops [21:20, 21:50].
- Lineup and substitution pattern analysis of opponents [24:23].
- G League as a testing ground [06:39].

## Limits and open questions

- Panelists are NBA and WNBA insiders (the moderator is a former player), speaking from experience, with no data shown.
- Adams's view that screening gravity is overblown is one player's opinion.
- The coachability scale is described as "pretty rough" [21:50].
- The caption skips the first audience question between 37:39 and 38:16.
- Speaker identity in several answers must be inferred from context because captions have no speaker labels; the answer to the final question (what to know on day one) is given by an unidentified panelist [43:55].
- Names are inconsistent in captions (Monte, Monty, Money; Ariana, Arianna; Sonia, Sonya).

## Q&A

- Mentorship and career path: Antonian and another panelist describe mentors who believed in them and gave honest feedback [38:46, 39:19, 39:49].
- Athleticism versus stats such as dunk rate: Antonian says they work together and discrepancies should be investigated with film [40:49, 41:20, 41:50].
- Large language models in front offices: McNair says learn what they do well and poorly, and start using them now [42:20, 42:51].
- One thing to know on day one: a panelist cites crashing the glass versus transition defense [43:55].

## Summary

Dr. James Naples, an ENT surgeon and educator at Harvard Medical School, argues that healthcare uses outcome and patient data well but barely measures the surgeon and the environment, which sports teams track routinely. Using a patient's Halloween remark as the starting point, he describes studies on birthdays, team familiarity, daylight savings, time of day for cancer treatment and left-handed equipment. He says sports analytics taught him to treat non-significant findings as possibly relevant and to explore outliers. He is working with a sports psychologist to build a sports-style analytics team in healthcare. Most studies are cited without names or data.

## Key claims

- A patient's worry that he would rush on Halloween to get home to his children changed how he thinks about data [04:39, 05:09].
- There is no data on how he performs on Halloween, but there is a Medicare study on surgeon birthdays showing worse outcomes [05:39, 06:10].
- Sports teams analyze the athlete and the environment; surgery analyzes outcomes and patient factors but not systematically the surgeon or system [06:40, 07:12, 07:43].
- Healthcare lacks the analytics teams sports have; he would have to pull and analyze data himself [07:43, 08:13].
- Papers treat the surgeon and environment as constants, which he says they are not [08:13].
- He describes healthcare as in a "moneyball" era without systematized data use [09:15].
- A cardiac surgery study shows that as team familiarity rises, surgical time falls and outcomes improve, more steeply for complex surgery [10:15, 10:45].
- Daylight savings affects patient health and marathon times; he suggests a biological clock effect and says healthcare does not account for it [11:47, 12:18].
- Capture systems account for only a small share of safety-related events [12:48].
- Cancer patients treated early in the day have higher three-year survival than those treated later [13:19].
- Left-handed surgeons are pushed out because left-handed equipment costs two to three times as much, and they are forced to use right-handed tools [13:50, 14:22, 14:53].
- Healthcare has a "p value problem": non-significant does not mean irrelevant [15:53].
- He now explores outliers with anomaly-seeking research rather than excluding them [16:25, 16:56, 17:26].
- Leading with behavior stories before data works better with clinicians; he works with a sports psychologist and wants a healthcare organization with performance psychologists and data analysts [17:56, 18:26, 18:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- About 400 surgeons do his specialty [01:01].
- Birthday study: almost a million surgeries from a Medicare database [06:10].
- A cardiac surgery study suggests up to 98% of outcome variability is due to the surgeon and system [08:43].
- Marathon runners about 12 minutes slower in spring than autumn around daylight savings [11:47].
- Safety event systems capture about 14% of events [12:48].
- Cancer time-of-day survival measured at 3 years [13:19].
- Left-handed equipment two to three times the cost [14:53].
- None of the studies are named in the captions; the 98% and 14% numbers could be caption errors and cannot be checked against the talk.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Retrospective database analysis (Medicare data, cardiac team studies) [06:10, 10:15].
- Anomaly-seeking research on outliers [16:25].
- Story-first communication with a sports psychologist, then data layered on [17:56].

## Limits and open questions

- No study is identified, and no effect sizes (other than those above) are shown.
- Halloween has no data behind it by his own account [05:39, 16:25].
- Time-of-day cancer result: a questioner raises possible administration or adherence explanations; Naples says studies are controlled for cancer type and degree and that scheduling barriers may exist [25:36, 26:07]. Whether timing causes the survival difference is not resolved.
- The West Coast travel point is his interpretation [12:18].
- Applicability to athletes is asserted by analogy, not shown.

## Q&A

- How long until enough research exists, and can LLMs help: depends on institutional effort; the data exists but databases have not been built to study these factors [19:56, 20:28, 20:59].
- Why insurers do not push this research: he has reached out to insurance liaisons and wonders whether physicians avoid publishing so insurers cannot use it against them [20:59, 21:29].
- Telematics-style pricing for physicians: people with bad outcomes would object [22:03, 22:34].
- Testing doctor knowledge and dexterity: surgery does not test dexterity before residency, and knowledge metrics are not consistent predictors beyond board passage [23:04, 23:35].
- Robotic surgery data: robots track hand and eye movements but that is proprietary; he has spoken with the company [24:36, 25:06].
- Alternative explanations for cancer timing: studies are controlled, but administrative barriers may exist [25:36, 26:07].
